# Background and objectives

Differential expression analysis is commonly used to study diverse
biological datasets. The reproducibility-optimized test statistic (ROTS)
([Elo et al., 2008](https://doi.org/10.1109/tcbb.2007.1078)) uses a
modified t-statistic to prioritise features that differ between two or
more groups. However, the ROTS Bioconductor implementation ([Suomi et
al., 2017](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005562)) did not
accommodate technical or biological covariates. LimROTS ([Anwar et al.,
2025](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btaf570)) addressed this
limitation by combining a reproducibility-optimized test statistic with
the limma empirical Bayes approach ([Ritchie et al.,
2015](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkv007)). This enables the analysis of
more complex experimental designs and the incorporation of covariates.
These validated solutions were made in Bioconductor development version
3.20 and the subsequent release 3.21. Related but different linear
modeling features were subsequently incorporated also into ROTS
Bioconductor package, but have not been formally published to our
knowledge. Both ROTS and LimROTS added linear model extensions for
survival analysis in the Bioconductor devel version 3.23.

## How to cite LimROTS

If you use `LimROTS` in your research, please cite:

> Anwar, A. M., Jeba, A., Lahti, L., & Coffey, E. (2025). LimROTS: A
> Hybrid Method Integrating Empirical Bayes and
> Reproducibility-Optimized Statistics for Robust Differential
> Expression Analysis. *Bioinformatics*, btaf570.
> <https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btaf570>

## Relationship to ROTS and limma

LimROTS is a standalone package that extends ROTS ([Elo et al.,
2008](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/4359873); [Tomi Suomi et al.,
2017](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005562))
and the limma ([Ritchie ME et al.,
2015](https://academic.oup.com/nar/article/43/7/e47/2414268)) framework.
It is a newly developed, independently implemented method that
incorporates covariates in reproducibility-optimized testing. LimROTS is
not affiliated with, endorsed by, or maintained by the original ROTS or
limma developers. Users are advised to cite the original publications
when referencing these methods.

ROTS: Elo LL, Filén S, Lahesmaa R, Aittokallio T.
Reproducibility-optimized test statistic for ranking genes in microarray
studies. IEEE/ACM Transactions on Computational Biology and
Bioinformatics. 2008;5(3):423–31.

Suomi T, Seyednasrollah F, Jaakkola MK, Faux T, Elo LL (2017) ROTS: An R
package for reproducibility-optimized statistical testing. PLOS
Computational Biology 13(5): e1005562.
<https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005562>

limma: Ritchie ME, Phipson B, Wu D, Hu Y, Law CW, Shi W, Smyth GK. limma
powers differential expression analyses for RNA-sequencing and
microarray studies. Nucleic Acids Research. 2015;43(7):e47.
<https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkv007>

## How LimROTS combines empirical Bayes from limma and reproducibility optimization

The **LimROTS** workflow proceeds as follows:

1.  A linear model is fitted to the data using a user-supplied design
    matrix via limma @limma.
2.  Empirical Bayes variance shrinkage is applied to obtain moderated
    statistics. The adjusted standard error for each feature is:
    $SE_{\text{post}} = \sqrt{s^2_{\text{post}}} \times \text{unscaled SD}$,
    along with the regression coefficient $\beta_{(p)}$.
3.  A reproducibility-optimization step selects parameters $\alpha_1$
    and $\alpha_2$ by maximizing the overlap of top-ranked features
    across group-preserving bootstrap datasets.
4.  The final statistic for each feature is:

$$t_{\alpha(p)} = \frac{\beta_{(p)}}{\alpha_1 + \alpha_2 \times SE_{\text{post}(p)}}$$

where $t_{\alpha(p)}$ is the optimized statistic, $\beta_{(p)}$ is the
model coefficient, and $SE_{\text{post}(p)}$ is the adjusted standard
error.

P-values are derived from permutation-based null distributions using the
`qvalue` package @qvalue. FDR is estimated using an internal
implementation adapted from ROTS @rots, and q-values are computed via
the bootstrap method for the proportion of true null hypotheses.

## Computational considerations

LimROTS runtime depends on four primary factors: the number of samples,
features, bootstrap iterations (`niter`), and the top list size (`K`).
The bootstrapping step is parallelized using `BiocParallel`
@BiocParallel; we recommend using at least 4 workers for routine
analyses. The optimization step is sequential and may be time-consuming
for large values of `K`.

## LimROTS function parameters

`LimROTS()` is the primary interface for end users. For a full
description of all parameters, refer to the function documentation:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
?LimROTS
```

# UPS1-spiked DIA proteomics case study

## Dataset design and sample metadata

This case study demonstrates LimROTS with a quantitative proteomics
dataset in which known UPS1 proteins are spiked into an *E. coli*
background @Gotti2021. Because the spike-in concentrations are known,
the data provide a useful setting for examining concentration-associated
differences while accounting for the DIA isolation-window setting.

The same experimental groups were measured using two DIA acquisition
settings: narrow and wide isolation windows. Each setting contains three
replicate samples for each of eight UPS1 concentration groups: A (0.1
fmol), B (0.25 fmol), C (1 fmol), D (2.5 fmol), E (5 fmol), F (10 fmol),
G (25 fmol), and H (50 fmol). The combined dataset therefore has 48
samples, with 24 samples per window.

The `HEof_DIA` object stores log2 MaxLFQ intensities in its
`log2_intensity` assay. Its sample metadata include the condition,
replicate, and DIA window. The two window-specific datasets are combined
by protein, and missing values are imputed separately within each window
using BPCA before combination. The dataset was adapted from @Peng2024.

This dataset is used for demonstration purposes; however, the same
workflow can be applied to real-world label-free DIA or DDA experiments.
In this example, the DIA isolation windows represent covariates that
mirror those encountered in real-world experiments, including biological
covariates (e.g., sex and age) and technical covariates (e.g., digestion
batches).

## Load and inspect the dataset

```{r load-packages, message=FALSE}
library(LimROTS, quietly = TRUE)
library(BiocParallel, quietly = TRUE)
library(ggplot2, quietly = TRUE)
library(SummarizedExperiment, quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r load-dataset}
data("HEof_DIA")
print(HEof_DIA)
```

```{r}
table(HEof_DIA$condition, HEof_DIA$window)
```

## Explore sample patterns with PCA

PCA provides an unsupervised, sample-level overview of the largest
patterns of variation in the protein-intensity data. Here, color
identifies the UPS1 concentration group and point shape identifies the
DIA isolation window. This makes it easier to visually assess whether
samples show patterns associated with the known concentration groups,
whether replicates appear similar, and whether the acquisition window is
associated with a broader shift in the data.

This PCA is exploratory: it does not test for differential abundance or
establish that a group or window caused an observed pattern. The LimROTS
analysis below addresses concentration-associated differences while
including the window as a covariate.

```{r}
data <- assay(HEof_DIA, "log2_intensity")
variable_proteins <- apply(data, 1, sd) > 0
pca <- prcomp(
  t(data[variable_proteins, , drop = FALSE]),
  center = TRUE
)

scores <- data.frame(
  PC1 = pca$x[, 1],
  PC2 = pca$x[, 2],
  as.data.frame(colData(HEof_DIA))
)
variance <- summary(pca)$importance[2, 1:2] * 100

ggplot(scores, aes(PC1, PC2, color = condition, shape = window)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73", "#CC79A7",
    "#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#F0E442", "#000000"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "PCA of narrow- and wide-window DIA samples",
    x = sprintf("PC1 (%.1f%%)", variance[1]),
    y = sprintf("PC2 (%.1f%%)", variance[2]),
    color = "Sample group",
    shape = "DIA window"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)

```

## Select two concentration groups for LimROTS

```{r}
CF_HEof_DIA <- HEof_DIA[, colData(HEof_DIA)$condition %in% c("C", "F")]
table(AF_HEof_DIA$condition, AF_HEof_DIA$window)
```

## Run LimROTS on the selected groups

Set a seed before running LimROTS to ensure reproducibility.

```{r set-seed}
set.seed(1234, kind = "default", sample.kind = "default")
```

> **Note:** The `group` column in `colData` must be a character vector,
> and `pairwise_contrasts` can be used to specify the contrasts, such as
> `conditionF-conditionC`.

```{r run-limrots}
# Define analysis parameters
meta.info   <- c("condition", "window")
niter       <- 100   # bootstrap iterations (use >= 1000 for real analyses)
K           <- 50   # top list size for reproducibility optimization
formula.str <- "~ 0 + condition + window"

# Run LimROTS
CF_HEof_DIA <- LimROTS(
  x           = CF_HEof_DIA,
  niter       = niter,
  K           = K,
  meta.info   = meta.info,
  group       = "condition",
  formula.str = formula.str,
  pairwise_contrasts = "conditionF-conditionC",
  trend       = TRUE,
  strata = c("window"),
  correlation_block = NULL,
  model = "limma",
  BPPARAM = SnowParam(workers = 2, progressbar = T)
)
```

> **Note:** `niter = 100` and `K = 100` are used here to reduce vignette
> build time. For real-world analyses, use `niter = 1000` or higher and
> `k = 25% of the feature count`, which is the default if not explicitly
> specified. We also recommend at least 4 parallel

To increase the number of workers, pass a `BPPARAM` argument:

```{r bpparam-example}
# Windows
# BPPARAM <- SnowParam(workers = 4)

# Linux / macOS
# BPPARAM <- MulticoreParam(workers = 4)

# Pass to LimROTS via: LimROTS(..., BPPARAM = BPPARAM)
```

The results are appended directly to the `rowData` and `metadata` slots
of the input `SummarizedExperiment` object.

## Visualize differential-abundance results

The volcano plot below shows corrected log-fold changes versus
$-\log_{10}$(q-value). At a 5% q-value threshold, LimROTS recovers the
majority of true UPS1 human proteins while flagging very few *E. coli*
proteins or zero.

```{r volcano-plot}
# Extract results
result_df <- data.frame(
    rowData(CF_HEof_DIA)
)

result_df$label <- ifelse(
  result_df$Organism == "UPS",
  "UPS1 (TP)",
  "E. coli (TN)"
)

result_df$significance <- ifelse(
  result_df$qvalue < 0.05,
  "FDR < 0.05",
  "Not significant"
)


q_cutoff <- max(result_df$pvalue[result_df$qvalue < 0.05], na.rm = TRUE)

ggplot(result_df, aes(
  x = corrected.logfc,
  y = -log10(pvalue),
  color = label,
  shape = label
)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8, stroke = 1) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = -log10(q_cutoff),
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.5,
    color = "grey30"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = Inf,
    y = -log10(q_cutoff),
    label = "q-value = 0.05",
    hjust = 1.1,
    vjust = -0.6,
    size = 3.5,
    color = "grey30"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dotted",
    color = "grey60",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "E. coli (TN)" = "#0072B2",
    "UPS1 (TP)" = "#D55E00"
  )) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(
    "E. coli (TN)" = 16,
    "UPS1 (TP)" = 1
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "LimROTS – C Vs. F HEof DIA dataset",
    x = expression("Corrected log"[2] * " fold change"),
    y = expression(-log[10](pvalue)),
    color = NULL,
    shape = NULL
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "top",
    axis.text = element_text(color = "black")
  )
```

# Adjusted p-values and FDR estimates in LimROTS

LimROTS reports four related but distinct measures in the feature-level
`rowData`: empirical `pvalue`s, Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted
`BH.pvalue`s, `qvalue`s estimated with the `qvalue` package @qvalue, and
a permutation-based `FDR`. The empirical p-values are calculated by
comparing each observed LimROTS statistic with the statistics from the
permuted null fits. `BH.pvalue` applies the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure
to these empirical p-values to adjust for testing many features.
Separately, `qvalue` estimates q-values from the empirical p-values,
estimating the proportion of true null hypotheses (`pi0`) with the
bootstrap method. The `FDR` column is estimated directly from the
permuted statistics. Thus, these columns are alternative summaries of
evidence and false-discovery control, not interchangeable versions of
the same adjusted p-value. Interpret the chosen measure consistently,
and state which one you use when reporting significance.

# How `strata` and `correlation_block` affect resampling in LimROTS

In LimROTS, `strata` controls how bootstrap and permutation samples are
grouped, while `correlation_block` identifies linked samples—usually
repeated measurements from the same person. 1. If both are NULL, samples
are bootstrapped within each group, and group labels are shuffled across
all samples for permutation. 2. If `strata` is supplied and
`correlation_block` is NULL, resampling and label shuffling happen
within the specified strata; the group column is excluded from the
strata. 3. If `strata` is NULL and `correlation_block` is supplied, the
block setting takes precedence: whole blocks are resampled together, and
permutations are done within blocks. For a before/after design, use a
subject ID column so each person’s two measurements stay paired. The
current bootstrap requires every block to have exactly one sample from
each of the two groups. With `model = "limma"`, the block is also used
to estimate within-block correlation. With `model = "dream"`, include
the block as a random effect in the formula, such as `(1 \| subject)`;
the formula models that effect, while the block setting controls
resampling. 4. If both are supplied, the code follows the
`correlation-block` branch, so `strata` is effectively ignored for
sampling and permutation.

```{r session-info}
sessionInfo()
```
